Categorize

/KAT-uh-guh-ryz/ - the stress falls on KAT · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Categorize means to sort things into groups by type.

The budgeting app categorizes each expense the moment it posts — fuel, groceries, rent — so tax season takes one afternoon.

Worked Example

The recycling depot's new hires spend their first week learning to categorize what pours off the trucks: glass by color, plastics by number, metals by magnet. A load that once went to one mountain of scrap now flows into eleven labeled bays.

Categorize fits because each item is assigned to a defined type with rules — not merely tidied. Sort would cover rough piles; group could be casual; categorize says the bins have names and every item belongs to exactly one.

How Categorize Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

sort

sort: the everyday word for splitting things into rough piles

group

group: gathers things loosely together, with or without a system

Antonyms

jumble

jumble: to mix everything together into disorder

scatter

scatter: to fling things apart with no order at all

How Strong Is It? — sort → categorize → index

sort vs. categorize

sort vs. categorize: Sorting is milder than categorize — it splits a heap into rough piles, while categorizing assigns each item to a defined, named type.

index vs. categorize

index vs. categorize: Index goes further than categorize: beyond grouping things by type, an index gives every single item its own findable entry.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — categor

Root — categor: a class of things (Greek kategoria, originally a charge declared in the assembly)

Suffix — -ize

Suffix — -ize: to make into, to treat by

Put it together

Put it together: Categor- (a class) + -ize (to make into) = to place things into classes. Greek kategoria began as a public accusation — a statement declaring what someone was — and philosophers borrowed it for statements declaring what anything is: its type, its class, its category.

Use the root in a new word: category

Use the root in a new word: category: Every entry at the county fair fits one category and only one, from pickles to pies.

Word Choice

neutral

Categorize is the workhorse for sorting by type: it implies the groups have names and rules. Sort is the everyday word for rough piles; reach for categorize when a system is doing the work — files, species, expenses, library shelves.
